proposal.rationale: Transfer hypothesis: adapt the cited PCB layout work into a Gerber/netlist review that connects geometric risk flags to measured emission hotspots. A checklist tied to specific traces and return paths could make layout corrections testable before the company's next external EMC visit. This is a proposed transfer, not proof of fewer failed tests. Confirm the researcher's contribution and rights to any existing implementation.

facts.quote: Three of our last five PCB designs failed radiated emissions at a third-party EMC lab on the first submission, typically between 150–450 MHz, which costs us on average €9,000 per re-test visit and delays client projects by six to ten weeks; we need a systematic way to predict and fix emission hotspots during layout review rather than after the fact.
We can allocate one senior hardware engineer and one firmware engineer part-time to a collaborative project, with access to our lab equipment and internal board archives under NDA.
Automated PCB Layout Scoring for EMC Risk Using Feature Extraction and a Rule-Based Engine

Manual EMC design review is time-consuming and relies on reviewer expertise that varies across organisations. This paper describes a rule-based layout scoring tool that ingests Gerber files and a netlist, extracts geometric features related to emission risk, and outputs a numerical score and flagged violation list. Seventeen rules were derived from simulation studies and published guidelines, covering trace-to-plane spacing, clock trace routing

plan.question: Can PCB layout rules flag actionable EMC hotspots before external testing? A follow-on industrial PhD could examine emission predictors across board families, subject to sufficient data, supervision and funding agreements.
plan.experiment: Propose a three-month feasibility pilot extracting trace/plane features and comparing a rule checklist with archived scans. Freeze rules before each held-out board; include passed boards and one prospective layout review. Output is engineering triage, not certification.
plan.metrics: Measure hotspot agreement with scans, false flags per board and engineer review time. Proposed gate: identify a plausible hotspot on every held-out failed board, with at most five actionable false flags per review; a small sample gives uncertain estimates. External lab success remains unproven.
plan.companyAsk: Request a layout engineer to annotate hotspots, assess manufacturability and reserve one review session weekly. Confirm board access and staffing.
plan.researcherAsk: Invite the researcher to map features to rules, interpret emission mechanisms and analyze held-out results. Confirm personal contribution, availability and code rights before reuse.
plan.dataRequired: Request NDA-protected Gerbers, netlists, stackups, BOMs and emission scans for passed and failed boards, with operating modes and scan conditions. Agree access and retention before transfer.
plan.milestones: Month 1 (weeks 1–4): company provides approved inventory and annotations; researcher delivers baseline checklist. Month 2 (weeks 5–8): researcher implements rules; company reviews held-out flags. Month 3 (weeks 9–12): jointly review a prospective layout and deliver scripts, evidence log and go/no-go recommendation.
plan.risks: A handful of boards cannot establish generalization. Enclosure, cables and operating mode can dominate emissions. Stop if netlists or scan conditions are unavailable; do not promise certification or avoided retest fees.
plan.meeting: In week 1, layout lead and researcher inspect approved failed/passed design examples, reserve held-out boards and assign scan annotations. Leave the meeting with a file checklist, baseline and dated budget/access decision.
plan.terms: Agree a capped feasibility fee or joint funding application only after scoping. Keep client designs confidential, separate background methods from new scripts, and negotiate prototype ownership and publication review.
